Name: Jumping
Description: The ability for the player character to leap off the ground. Jumping is a fundamental movement allowing the player to overcome obstacles and reach higher platforms.
Implementation Details: Implemented by applying an upward velocity or impulse to the character when the jump input is detected, typically only if the character is on the ground (to avoid infinite jumps). Key considerations include setting a proper jump velocity, applying gravity to bring the player back down, and possibly allowing for variable jump height (e.g., a longer button press yields a higher jump). It's also common to implement a short grace period for jumping after leaving a ledge (coyote time) to make the game feel more responsive.

Name: Double Jump
Description: Allows the player to jump a second time in mid-air before landing. This gives the player extra reach and agility for platforming.
Implementation Details: Typically implemented by tracking the number of jumps performed since the last time the player was on the ground. The player can initiate a second jump even if not on ground, resetting or incrementing a jump counter. Once the double jump is used, further jumps are disallowed until the player lands. Design considerations include whether multiple jumps are allowed (double, triple, etc.), and providing visual or audio feedback for the second jump.

Name: Wall Jump
Description: Enables the player to jump off a wall to reach new areas or climb upwards by alternating between walls. The player typically needs to be in contact with a wall (while in the air) and then jump, which propels them away from the wall.
Implementation Details: Implement by detecting when the player is against a wall and not on the ground. This can be done by checking collisions on the player's sides. When the jump input is pressed while touching a wall, invert the player's horizontal velocity away from the wall and give an upward boost. Often combined with a wall slide mechanic to give the player time to execute the wall jump. It's important to reset any jump counters (for double jump) upon wall jump or handle it so it doesn't allow infinite climbing by abusing double jump and wall contact.

Name: Wall Slide
Description: When the player character presses against a vertical surface (wall) in mid-air, their fall is slowed, allowing them to slide down the wall. This gives the player more control and time to plan a wall jump or descent.
Implementation Details: Check if the player is against a wall and moving downward without being on the ground. If so, reduce the downward velocity (or apply a slight upward force) to slow the fall. In Phaser, this might involve setting a smaller gravity or directly capping the velocity when against a wall. Also, typically the player's animation changes to a sliding pose. A wall slide is often a precursor state to enable a wall jump.

Name: Dashing
Description: A quick burst of movement in a specified direction (often horizontal) that allows the player to cover ground rapidly or dodge hazards. Dashes are usually short and may include a brief period of invincibility.
Implementation Details: Implement by listening for a dash input and then temporarily increasing the player's velocity or moving their position in the desired direction. In Phaser, you might set the player's velocityX to a high value for a short duration or use a tween to move the player. It's common to disable normal movement control during the dash and possibly give the player invulnerability frames. After dashing, enforce a cooldown before the player can dash again.

Name: Sliding
Description: The player can slide along the ground, often to get through low tunnels or avoid obstacles. Usually triggered by pressing down (crouch) while running, causing the character to drop and slide forward a short distance.
Implementation Details: When the input for slide is detected (typically down or crouch while moving), switch the player to a sliding state: adjust the player's hitbox to be lower, set a fixed horizontal velocity, and possibly reduce friction so the player slides. After a set duration or distance, return the player to normal. Ensure the player cannot slide again until the first slide ends (to prevent spamming). Often accompanied by a unique animation and lower collision profile.

Name: Flying
Description: Allows the player to move freely in the air for an extended period or indefinitely, essentially negating gravity. This could be via a jetpack, wings, or other power-ups, and is typically limited by a resource (fuel, stamina) or time.
Implementation Details: Implement by toggling or reducing gravity's effect on the player when the fly mode is activated. The player can then be given control to move up/down as well as horizontally while flying. For example, pressing the jump button could apply an upward force continuously, or simply allow free movement in all directions. Make sure to handle transitions between flying and normal state (re-enable gravity when done). Also manage any resource (like fuel) if flight is limited.

Name: Climbing
Description: The ability to climb up and down ladders or other climbable surfaces. When on a ladder, the player can move vertically (and sometimes horizontally if it's a climbing wall) at a controlled speed, often while gravity is disabled.
Implementation Details: Implement by defining specific objects or areas as climbable. When the player overlaps or collides with a ladder, switch the player's mode to a climbing state: disable gravity and allow up/down movement. Typically, horizontal movement is either disabled or limited while climbing. Once the player exits the ladder (jumping off or reaching the end), re-enable gravity and return control to normal. You may also need to snap the player to the ladder's X position for a clean climbing alignment.

Name: Swimming
Description: A movement mode for when the player is underwater or in a liquid. The player's movement typically becomes slower and gravity is reduced or negated, allowing buoyant movement up and down through the fluid with more drag.
Implementation Details: Implement by detecting when the player enters a water area (using overlap or a tile property). Once in water, adjust physics properties: lower gravity or even invert it slightly for buoyancy, and increase drag or reduce movement speed. The jump input can be repurposed to swim upwards (apply upward velocity), while not pressing anything lets the player slowly sink. Often, an oxygen mechanic is added (a timer for how long the player can stay underwater). On exiting the water, restore normal gravity and movement settings.

Name: Crouching
Description: Allows the player to duck or crouch, reducing their height. This is useful for avoiding low-hanging obstacles or enemy attacks, and sometimes to initiate other actions like sliding or dropping through platforms.
Implementation Details: Implement by listening for a down input when the player is on the ground. On crouch, change the player's collider height (and possibly width) to a smaller size and adjust the sprite/animation. The player's movement speed might be reduced while crouching. If the game has one-way platforms (that can be dropped through), combining down + jump could let the player drop down through the platform. Ensure to prevent the player from standing up if an obstacle is overhead (to avoid getting stuck in a wall).

Name: Melee Attack
Description: A close-range attack typically executed by the player using a weapon (like a sword) or their body (punch, kick). Melee attacks usually require the player to be near an enemy to deal damage.
Implementation Details: Implement by listening for an attack input, then triggering an attack animation and detecting collisions or overlaps with enemy hitboxes during that animation. In Phaser, you might create an attack hitbox (an Arcade Physics body or use the player's body extended) that is active for a few frames. When an enemy overlaps this hitbox, reduce the enemy's health. You may also briefly disable movement or allow only limited movement during the attack. Consider combos (chaining multiple attacks) and cooldowns between attacks to balance gameplay.

Name: Ranged Attack
Description: An attack performed from a distance, usually by firing a projectile (like an arrow, bullet, or magic spell). Ranged attacks allow the player to hit targets far away, often with a trade-off like limited ammo or lower damage.
Implementation Details: Implement by creating a projectile object when the attack input is pressed. In Phaser, you can use a physics group for bullets or arrows. When the player uses a ranged attack, spawn a projectile sprite at the player's position (with possibly an offset from the weapon) and give it a velocity toward the target direction (e.g., left or right based on player facing). Handle collisions between the projectile and enemies: on collision, reduce enemy health and destroy the projectile. Manage resources like ammo or cooldowns if needed to prevent spamming.

Name: Counter / Parry
Description: A defensive move where the player times an input (or uses a specific move) to counter an enemy's attack, often negating the damage and stunning the enemy or dealing a return blow. This usually requires precise timing.
Implementation Details: Implement by defining a short window during which a counter action is active. For instance, if the player hits a parry button, for the next few frames the player is in a counter state. If an enemy attack hits the player during this state, the attack is negated and the enemy is stunned or takes damage. In Phaser, you might set a flag `player.isParrying = true` for a brief time and check collisions differently during that period (like if player overlaps an enemy attack hitbox while parrying). You also often play a special animation for the parry. After the window, if no attack was parried, the player may be left vulnerable for a moment to balance the mechanic.

Name: Dodging
Description: An evasive maneuver that allows the player to avoid enemy attacks or hazards, usually by quickly moving out of the way or becoming temporarily invincible. This can be a roll, slide, or short teleport depending on the game.
Implementation Details: Implement by listening for a dodge input and then executing a quick movement or state change. One common approach is a dodge-roll where the player moves a short distance quickly and is invulnerable during the roll. In Phaser, you can simulate this by setting a velocity or tweening the player's position for the dodge duration and toggling an invincibility flag or property (like ignoring collisions) briefly. After the dodge, restore the normal state. Ensure there's a brief cooldown so the player cannot dodge continuously without consequence.

Name: Blocking
Description: A defensive mechanic where the player uses a shield or simply braces to reduce or negate damage from incoming attacks, at the cost of some stamina or other resource. While blocking, the player usually cannot attack, and movement might be limited.
Implementation Details: Implement by allowing the player to hold a block button which puts them in a blocking state. In this state, adjust damage calculation for collisions: e.g., if an enemy attack hits the player while blocking, either reduce damage or nullify it and perhaps reduce a stamina meter instead. In Phaser, you might have a flag `player.isBlocking` and check it in the enemy collision logic. Also, typically the player can't block indefinitely — a stamina or guard meter can deplete with each block, or heavy attacks break the guard.

Name: Combo System
Description: A combat mechanic allowing the player to chain multiple attacks in sequence with varying outcomes. Each successive attack in a combo might have a different animation or effect, encouraging rhythmic button presses rather than spamming a single attack.
Implementation Details: Implement by tracking the timing and sequence of attack inputs. For example, if the player presses the attack button within a short window after the first attack, trigger a second attack animation, and then a third, etc. In Phaser, you can manage this by listening for input during or right after an attack animation. Use a state or counter for the current combo step, and reset it if too much time passes or the combo completes. Also ensure that hitting an enemy possibly resets or affects the combo (some games only allow continued combo if previous hit connected). Balancing involves deciding how many hits a combo has and the total damage vs single attacks.

Name: Shops / Purchasing Items
Description: Locations or interfaces where the player can buy items, equipment, or upgrades using in-game currency. Shops allow players to exchange collected currency (coins, gems, etc.) for various benefits.
Implementation Details: Implement by creating a shop entity (like an NPC or a menu) that the player can interact with. When triggered (e.g., player presses an interact key near a shopkeeper), pause the game action and bring up a shop UI listing items for sale with their prices. In Phaser, this could involve displaying text and graphics for items and listening for input to select an item. Check the player's currency amount, and if they have enough, deduct the cost and grant the item (adding to inventory or applying an upgrade). Key considerations include managing the shop inventory (static list of items or dynamic), and ensuring the player can't buy if they lack funds. Provide feedback on successful purchase or insufficient funds.

Name: Stat Upgrades
Description: Permanent improvements to the player's attributes such as health, attack power, defense, speed, etc. Stat upgrades make the character stronger or more capable and are usually earned through leveling up, finding collectibles, or purchasing in shops.
Implementation Details: Implement by maintaining variables for player stats (e.g., maxHealth, attackPower, speed). When a stat upgrade occurs, increment these values. This can happen via different methods: experience points and levels (where reaching a new level increases stats), picking up a specific upgrade item (like a heart container to increase max health), or buying an upgrade from a shop. In Phaser, applying an upgrade might simply be a matter of changing those variables and perhaps updating UI elements (like health bar length). Ensure that any stat changes are applied immediately (e.g., if max health increases, you might also heal the player or not, depending on design). It's also important to cap stats or balance upgrades so the game remains challenging.

Name: Inventory System
Description: A system allowing the player to carry and manage items (weapons, potions, keys, etc.). The player can pick up items into an inventory, switch between them, or use them when needed. Inventories can have limited slots or weight, or be unlimited.
Implementation Details: Implement by having a data structure (like an array or object) to store items the player has collected. Each item could be an object with properties (name, type, quantity, etc.). In Phaser, you might not see the inventory on screen unless an inventory UI is opened. You will handle item pickup events: when the player collides with an item on the ground, add it to the inventory and remove it from the world. Also handle using items: e.g., if the player selects a potion from the inventory and uses it, apply its effect (heal, etc.) and subtract one from the inventory. Key considerations include how the player navigates the inventory (keyboard, mouse, controller), and if there are limits (like max items).

Name: Power-ups
Description: Temporary or situational upgrades the player can collect that grant special abilities or enhancements. Examples include invincibility stars, damage boosts, jump height increases, or speed boosts, often lasting for a short duration or until hit.
Implementation Details: Implement by placing power-up items in the level that the player can pick up (like any collectible). When picked up, trigger an effect: modify the player's state or stats (e.g., set player.invulnerable = true, or player.speed += X) and often set a timer for when the effect wears off. In Phaser, on overlap with the power-up sprite, apply the effect and destroy the power-up object. Use a timed event for expiration: after time ends, revert the player's stats to normal. Visual or audio indicators (like a special color or sound while powered up) help communicate the effect. Consider making the power-up mutually exclusive or stackable carefully to avoid balancing issues.

Name: Ammo & Reload
Description: A mechanic that limits the use of ranged weapons by requiring ammunition and occasionally reloading. The player must manage ammo for guns or similar weapons, and if they run out, they cannot fire until they pick up more or reload if applicable.
Implementation Details: Implement by giving the player an ammo count for relevant weapons. Each time a ranged attack is fired, decrement the ammo. If ammo reaches zero, prevent firing. For weapons that reload (like a gun magazine), you can have a max ammo per clip and a reload function that takes some time to reset ammo (if the game design includes that detail). In Phaser, simply track ammo as a variable and maybe display it on the UI. On picking up ammo packs, increase the ammo count. If reloading, you might disable shooting for a short duration while playing a reload animation or sound.

Name: Crafting
Description: Allows the player to create new items or tools from collected resources. The player can combine materials (like wood, stone, etc.) according to recipes to craft weapons, potions, or other useful items. Common in survival or sandbox-style platformers.
Implementation Details: Implement by defining recipes that map required ingredients to an output item. The player needs an interface (e.g., a crafting menu or a crafting station in-game) to select a recipe and craft if they have the necessary materials in their inventory. In Phaser, you might manage this via a UI scene or overlay listing craftable items and checking the player's inventory counts. Upon crafting, subtract the used materials and add the crafted item to the inventory. Key considerations include how the player discovers recipes (they might be known from start or learned via pickups or NPCs) and ensuring the crafting process doesn't interrupt gameplay too much (maybe restrict crafting to safe zones).

Name: Equipment System
Description: A system where the player can equip items (weapons, armor, accessories) that alter their abilities or stats. Unlike a simple inventory item, an equipped item actively changes the player's attributes or available moves.
Implementation Details: Implement by allowing certain inventory items to be marked as 'equippable'. Provide a way for the player to choose which equipment to wear or use (e.g., selecting a sword or armor from the inventory). In Phaser, you might just change the player's stats or sprite when equipment is changed. For example, equipping a sword might set the player's attack damage to a certain value or enable a new attack animation; equipping an armor could increase defense or health. Ensure that only one item per slot is equipped at a time (like one weapon, one armor, etc.), and swap accordingly. It's also useful to show the equipped items on the UI and reflect changes immediately in gameplay (like new attack animations or different projectile for a new gun).

Name: Survival Mechanics
Description: Gameplay elements that require the player to manage resources to stay alive beyond just avoiding enemies. This often includes systems like hunger, thirst, fatigue, temperature, or other environmental conditions that the player must monitor and maintain.
Implementation Details: Implement by introducing additional player stats such as hunger or thirst meters that deplete over time. In Phaser (or any engine), you'd decrement these values on a timer or based on actions. For example, every few seconds reduce the hunger stat; if it falls to 0, the player might start losing health. Provide ways to replenish these, like consuming food or water items (which ties into an inventory system). You might also include environmental effects: e.g., if the player is in a cold area without a heat source, a 'warmth' meter could drop. Design considerations: ensure the player has fair access to resources and that the survival aspect adds challenge without becoming too tedious. Feedback (like flashing warnings or slowing the player when starving) is important.

Name: Health System
Description: The mechanics governing the player's life or hit points. This includes how much damage the player can take (hit points or health), how health is displayed (hearts, bar, number), and how the player can recover health (health pickups, regeneration) or lose it through damage.
Implementation Details: Implement by assigning a health value to the player (and enemies). In Phaser, you'd have something like player.health and player.maxHealth. Whenever the player collides with harmful objects or enemies, subtract damage from health. If health reaches zero, trigger the player's death or game over routine. Health can be visualized via a UI (like a health bar or icons). Health pickups (like medkits or heart items) can restore health when collected. Also consider invincibility frames after taking damage to prevent immediate multiple hits. For different styles: some games use a few 'hits' (like 3 hearts) rather than a numeric bar, but the concept is similar. Adjust difficulty by how frequent health refills are and how much damage enemies do.

Name: Wall Climbing
Description: Allows the player character to climb vertically along walls by clinging onto them. When next to a wall, the player can latch on and move up or down slowly, expanding exploration to vertical spaces without requiring ladders. Design considerations: Wall climbing should often be limited by stamina or specific wall types so it doesn't bypass level design intended for other challenges. Player feedback such as a dedicated wall-grab animation, dust particles when latching on, and slower movement while climbing communicates the mechanic clearly. Care must be taken to ensure the player can't exploit wall climbing to reach unintended areas or get stuck.
Implementation Details: In Phaser.js (using Arcade physics), you can detect when the player is touching a wall using the physics body's blocked or touching properties. For example, if `player.body.blocked.left` or `...right` is true, the player is against a wall. When the up or down input is pressed while against a wall, temporarily reduce or nullify gravity on the player and allow a controlled vertical velocity for climbing. Typically, you'll set a flag like `isClimbing` to true, set `player.setGravityY(0)` to prevent falling, and then apply `player.setVelocityY` to let the player move up/down at a set climb speed. If the player releases the wall or reaches the top, restore normal gravity. Also implement a slight downward slide when no climb input is given to simulate gravity, unless fully stopped.

Name: Grappling Hook
Description: Enables the player to fire a grappling hook to latch onto surfaces and quickly pull themselves towards that point or swing from it. This mechanic extends the player's range of movement, allowing them to reach high or far platforms that normal jumps can't. Design considerations: Grappling hooks should be limited to certain grapple points or have a cooldown to maintain challenge; otherwise players might bypass obstacles too easily. Provide clear visual cues (like dedicated grapple points or a visible rope line) and feedback (sound of the hook firing and attaching) to make usage intuitive. One challenge is handling the physics of the swing or pull smoothly so the player momentum feels natural without clipping through walls.
Implementation Details: In Phaser.js, implementing a grappling hook can be done via either a simple approach or using the physics engine. One approach is raycasting or checking a line from the player to the target direction to find a collidable surface (Phaser doesn't have built-in raycast in Arcade, but you can iterate along a vector or use Matter physics raycast). Upon hitting a valid surface, you would create a visual rope (using `Phaser.GameObjects.Line` or a chain of small segments) from the player to the hook point. You can then simulate pulling the player by disabling player gravity and setting velocity towards the hook point (using `player.setVelocity()` toward the target). For a swing effect (if using Matter physics), you could use a constraint: attach the player body to the anchor point with `Matter.Constraint` to allow realistic pendulum motion. After reaching the target or when the player cancels, remove the constraint or reset gravity to regain normal control.

Name: Stealth Mechanics
Description: Introduces gameplay where the player avoids detection by enemies through hiding, sneaking, or staying out of sight. For example, the player might crouch to hide in tall grass or stick to shadows to not be seen by guards. Design considerations: Stealth changes the pace of the game, offering a non-combat way to overcome challenges. Enemies should have clear detection indicators (like vision cones or alertness states) so the player knows when they're at risk. Balance is key: being stealthy should be rewarding (perhaps allowing the player to bypass a tough enemy or perform a silent takedown), but getting caught should trigger a reasonable consequence (like a chase or alarm). Ensure the environment supports stealth with areas to hide and a feedback mechanism (like the player sprite dimming or an icon when hidden) so the player knows they're concealed.
Implementation Details: In Phaser.js, stealth can be implemented by combining player state management and enemy AI logic. For instance, you might give enemies a 'vision range' and 'view cone' and use a line-of-sight calculation (raycasting to the player position to check if walls obstruct view). Alternatively, simpler: check distance and whether the player is in a 'visible' state. If the player is crouching or in a designated hiding spot (could be marked by a zone or a property on a tile/sprite), set a flag `player.isHidden = true`. Enemies in their update loop can skip or reduce detection if that flag is true. You might implement enemy patrols that periodically check: if player within a certain radius and `!player.isHidden`, then trigger alert. Use Arcade overlap checks for hiding spots (e.g., a transparent object that on overlap toggles player hidden state). This is largely logic rather than physics – also consider lowering player movement speed when sneaking for realism.

Name: Rope Swinging
Description: Allows the player to grab onto a hanging rope or vine and swing across gaps or obstacles. The rope is typically fixed at one end (like hanging from a tree or ceiling), and the player uses momentum to swing and then jump off to reach otherwise inaccessible areas. Design considerations: Rope swinging adds a physics-driven challenge; it should feel intuitive (perhaps automatically grab the rope if the player jumps to it) and fun. Make sure ropes are placed where needed and possibly have a bit of forgiveness in grab detection (a slightly larger grab range or auto-attach) to reduce frustration. Player feedback like the rope swaying visibly and a swinging animation helps convey momentum. Also ensure the player can't swing indefinitely to break level sequence (maybe the rope exists to get from A to B primarily).
Implementation Details: In Phaser, rope swinging can be implemented using physics (especially with Matter physics for realism). For Arcade physics, a simpler approach is to treat the rope as a point that, when grabbed, puts the player into a special swing state. In this state, you can simulate pendulum motion: perhaps by rotating the player around the rope's anchor point. Without true rotational physics in Arcade, you might manually update player's velocity or position along a circular path. Alternatively, using Matter.js, you could create a chain of constraint-linked bodies for the rope and attach the player body with a constraint joint to the rope's end upon grabbing, letting physics handle the swinging. On the code side, detect overlap or collision between the player and a rope end. On grab, disable player's gravity or normal controls and then either attach a physics constraint or run a timed swinging animation (calculating x,y via sin/cos for swing). When the player jumps off, remove the constraint or exit the swing state, re-enable gravity, and impart the player's body with the rope's momentum (velocity) to propel them.

Name: Time Manipulation
Description: Gives the player control over time as a gameplay element. This can manifest as slowing down time (temporary slow-motion), freezing time completely, or even reversing time to undo actions. With time manipulation, players can navigate otherwise impossible sequences (like dodging a flurry of obstacles in slow-mo or rewinding a missed jump). Design considerations: This is a powerful ability, so it often comes with limits such as a short duration, a cooldown, or specific locations where it can be used. Visual and audio feedback is crucial – e.g., a sepia tone or motion blur during slow-mo, and distinct sound effects when time is altered – so the player clearly feels the change. Implementing reverse time is complex (you'll need to record states); if included, make sure to communicate what can and cannot be rewound (usually everything or just the player). Balance puzzles around the mechanic to avoid trivializing challenges.
Implementation Details: In Phaser.js, slowing time can be achieved by adjusting the game's time scale. Phaser 3 allows you to modify `scene.time.timeScale` or the physics world step speed (for Arcade physics `scene.physics.world.timeScale`) to globally slow down or speed up the passage of time. For freezing time, you might simply pause the physics or use `scene.pause()` for a brief period (while still allowing player input for some cool effects, depending on design). Rewinding time is more complicated: you'd have to store snapshots of game state (player position, velocities, maybe enemy states) every frame or so. To implement a rewind, on activation stop normal updates and instead step backwards through the saved states, applying them to objects. This requires a lot of memory and careful syncing of state, but can be simplified by limiting what is affected (e.g., only the player's movement rewinds or certain puzzle objects reset).

Name: Magnetic Surfaces
Description: Introduces magnetism as a force affecting the player or objects. Certain surfaces or objects become magnetic, attracting (or repelling) the player or metal items. For example, the player might have magnetic boots that let them walk on a metal ceiling, or a magnet gun that pulls collectible metal objects from a distance. Design considerations: Magnetic areas must be clearly distinguished (e.g., color-coded or with metal textures) so players know when magnetism will apply. If the player can toggle magnetism, there should be an indicator for when it's active. Be cautious with physics: strong magnetic pulls can make controls unpredictable, so fine-tune the force strength. Also, limit the use to intended scenarios (like specific puzzle setups) to prevent sequence breaking (e.g., don't let player stick to every wall unless the game is designed around it). This mechanic can enable unique puzzles (like moving metal blocks by attracting them or flipping gravity for the player when on a magnetic surface).
Implementation Details: Implementing magnetic effects in Phaser depends on the physics system. With Arcade physics, you can simulate a magnetic pull by applying a continuous force towards or away from the magnetic source when the player or object is in range. Arcade doesn't have real forces, but you can adjust velocity or acceleration. For instance, if the player is near a magnetic ceiling and magnetism is enabled, set `player.body.allowGravity = false` and slowly move the player upward toward the surface (simulate attraction). Alternatively, if a 'magnet power' attracts a metal object (like an item or enemy with a flag), in the update loop calculate the vector towards the player and do `metal.body.velocity.x += (dx/distance) * force` to pull it in. With Matter physics, you could use `Body.applyForce` for more realistic gradual acceleration. Also manage state: e.g., `player.hasMagnetBoots` or `player.magnetActive` to toggle magnetic behavior. Ensure to re-enable gravity or stop forces when out of range or deactivated to return to normal physics.

Name: Teleportation
Description: Allows the player or objects to instantaneously move from one location to another. This often appears as teleportation portals in the level (step into one portal and emerge from another) or as a player ability to 'blink' a short distance. Teleportation enables creative level designs where direct movement is blocked but teleporters provide alternate routes; it can also serve as a quick travel mechanism in puzzles or combat escapes. Design considerations: Teleportation can easily bypass content, so restrict it appropriately (for example, fixed portal locations rather than free teleport, or line-of-sight blink). Ensure the player doesn't get disoriented: use visual cues like distinct portal colors and a brief pause or effect during teleport so the change in position is noticeable but not confusing. If it's a player-triggered ability, include a cooldown or resource cost. Also consider interaction with other mechanics, e.g., what happens if an enemy follows through a portal, or carrying objects through teleporters.
Implementation Details: In Phaser, implementing portals is straightforward with overlap events and position setting. You can create portal objects (e.g., sprites with a 'portal' tag or a specific group). Each portal might have a linked identifier to pair it with its destination. On overlap (`this.physics.add.overlap(player, portal, ...)`), you handle the teleport by setting `player.x` and `player.y` to the destination portal's coordinates. It helps to add a slight delay or toggle a flag to avoid instant re-teleporting if the destination overlaps the player with the portal immediately. For player-initiated teleport (blink), check input and determine target: for example, cast a ray or simply take the player's facing direction and desired distance, then `player.setPosition(newX, newY)`. Make sure to validate the target (not inside walls; you might do a `physics.world.overlap` check or tile collision check at the target point). You might temporarily disable collisions or input right after teleport to prevent issues. Add particle effects at the departure and arrival locations (Phaser has ParticleEmitter that you can trigger) and maybe a sound.

Name: Walking
Description: Standard, slow-paced forward movement. Often the default movement speed. In some games, walking is triggered when input is only partially engaged or when there is no sprint action active.
Implementation Details: In 2D or 3D, the player typically has a base speed for walking. When the player holds the movement input (e.g., arrow keys or joystick) slightly, the character moves at a slower, controlled pace. Walking is usually the default movement state before sprinting or other faster actions.

Name: Running/Sprinting
Description: A faster movement mode than walking, often activated by holding a specific button or fully tilting an analog stick. May consume stamina or limit other actions.
Implementation Details: Implemented by increasing the player's movement speed beyond the walking speed. In some games, sprinting is time-limited or cancels certain actions (like aiming). You might have a stamina bar that depletes during sprinting and regenerates when not sprinting.

Name: Crouching
Description: A lower posture that reduces the character’s height and noise output. It often allows passing through lower gaps or hiding behind cover more effectively.
Implementation Details: In a platformer or 3D game, implement by changing the player’s collider or hitbox height and possibly reducing movement speed. In Phaser, you can adjust body size. Crouching might also disable certain actions (like jumping, in some designs) or slow them.

Name: Crawling/Prone
Description: Fully lying down to move under very tight spaces or remain hidden. Movement speed is significantly reduced, but visibility and noise are minimized.
Implementation Details: Similar to crouching, but with an even smaller hitbox and slower movement. Some games only allow crawling in specific areas or require toggling a prone state. In Phaser, adjust the sprite/animation and collider to a minimal height.

Name: Sliding
Description: A quick, momentum-based move where the character goes low to the ground. Often initiated from sprinting or running, used to go under obstacles or quickly move into cover.
Implementation Details: When the player is sprinting and the slide input is triggered, set the player’s collider to a crouched state and apply a horizontal force to maintain momentum for a short duration. Typically, friction slows the player until the slide ends. This can transition into a crouch or stand when complete.

Name: Dodging/Evading (Short Hop/Roll)
Description: A quick evasive action, often a roll or hop, used to avoid attacks or hazards. Frequently grants brief invulnerability frames, enabling the player to bypass danger.
Implementation Details: Triggered by an input (e.g., a dodge button). Temporarily override the player’s normal movement, apply a quick dash or roll animation, and possibly grant invulnerability. In a platformer, this might be a short hop with horizontal velocity. Must ensure it has a cooldown or uses stamina to prevent spamming.

Name: Drifting
Description: Sideways skidding or sliding with momentum. In racing games, it helps maintain speed while cornering; in character action games, it can be a stylized sideways move.
Implementation Details: In racing, the player triggers a drift by holding a drift button and turning. The vehicle or character then slides sideways, with traction reduced and direction control altered. In Phaser, you might reduce friction and rotate the sprite while applying lateral velocity.

Name: Vaulting
Description: A quick hop or leap over a low obstacle without stopping. Common in parkour or shooters where fluid movement over barriers is needed.
Implementation Details: Detect a low obstacle in front of the player and, upon input, transition the character over it smoothly. This may be a simple jump with a different animation or a separate vaulting state. In Phaser, you can programmatically move the player’s position over the obstacle, or apply an arc to simulate hopping over.

Name: Jump (Basic)
Description: A standard upward leap to overcome gaps or obstacles. Often the simplest and most fundamental form of vertical movement.
Implementation Details: On button press, apply an upward velocity to the player if they are on the ground. Gravity pulls them back down. Consider a brief window or requirement (like must be onFloor) so as not to allow infinite air jumps.

Name: Variable Jump Height
Description: Alters the jump height based on how long the jump button is held. A quick press yields a shorter jump; holding the button results in a higher jump.
Implementation Details: Detect when the jump button is released. If the character is still moving upward, reduce vertical velocity to shorten the jump. This simulates a shorter leap if the button is tapped briefly.

Name: Double Jump / Multi-Jump
Description: Allows the player to jump again in mid-air, providing extra height or maneuverability. Some games extend this beyond two jumps for more advanced mobility.
Implementation Details: Keep track of how many jumps have been performed since leaving the ground. Once the allowed jump count is exceeded, no further air jumps are possible. Reset the count upon landing.

Name: Wall Jump
Description: Jumping off a wall to gain extra height or change direction. The player must be in contact with a wall before leaping away.
Implementation Details: Detect if the player’s side is colliding with a wall while in mid-air. On jump input, push the player away from the wall and upward. Often pairs well with a ‘wall slide’ mechanic so the player has time to input a jump.

Name: Wall Run
Description: Temporarily running along vertical surfaces. The player can traverse a wall for a short distance before leaping away or reaching a ledge.
Implementation Details: When the player hits a wall at sufficient speed and holds a specific input, reduce gravity or apply a horizontal velocity along the wall. A timer or stamina bar often limits the duration of the wall run. Jumping off resets normal physics.

Name: Climbing / Mantling
Description: Allows the player to ascend walls, ladders, or ledges. Often involves a dedicated animation to pull the character up once they're close to a ledge.
Implementation Details: Detect if the player is near a climbable surface. Transition to a climbing state, overriding movement to move vertically up the surface or mantle onto the ledge. Often slower than jumping but more reliable.

Name: Ledge Hang / Shimmy
Description: Hanging from a ledge and moving horizontally along it. This offers a safer way to traverse edges or avoid falling.
Implementation Details: When the player is close to a ledge (usually checks at the character’s hands or upper body), transition into a hanging state. Horizontal movement is slowed, restricted to a small range, until the player climbs up or drops.

Name: Pogo Jump
Description: Bouncing off enemies or objects to gain extra height or maintain aerial momentum. Holding the downward attack or jump key when over an enemy/object triggers the bounce.
Implementation Details: Detect collision or overlap with a valid bounce target while the player is in the air and a certain input is held. Reverse or boost the vertical velocity to simulate a bounce. This can chain multiple bounces if timed correctly.

Name: Rocket Jump
Description: Using an explosive force (e.g., firing a rocket at the ground) to propel oneself upwards. Often causes self-damage but grants significant height or distance.
Implementation Details: Check if the player fires an explosive weapon at the ground near their position. Apply upward and/or outward velocity to the player based on the explosion force. Subtract health or apply damage. This is more common in shooters, but can be adapted to 2D platformers with an explosive mechanism.

Name: Air Dash
Description: A short burst of movement while in mid-air, typically horizontal or angled. Offers quick repositioning or a way to close gaps.
Implementation Details: On input, temporarily override normal velocity with a dash vector. In 2D platformers, it's often purely horizontal. In some games, you can dash diagonally. Commonly has limited uses before landing or uses a cooldown/stamina system.

Name: Hero Landing / Ground Pound
Description: A slam into the ground from mid-air, dealing damage or creating an impact effect. Frequently used to break through fragile floors or stun nearby enemies.
Implementation Details: When the player is in mid-air and an input is held, set a high downward velocity. On collision with the ground (or enemy), trigger an effect (e.g., damage, area knockback, or breaking platforms).

Name: Grappling Hook / Zipline
Description: Firing a tether or hook to a surface or anchor point, then pulling yourself toward it or moving along it. Useful for crossing large gaps or quickly scaling heights.
Implementation Details: First, detect a valid grapple target within range and line of sight. Upon firing, create a tether line from the player to the target. Either set the player’s velocity towards the anchor or smoothly interpolate the player’s position along the line. For a zipline, detect when the player is near a zipline cable, then attach them so they slide along it under gravity or a set speed.

Name: Teleportation
Description: Instantly relocating the character to another point, bypassing normal movement. Can be limited by distance, cooldown, or specific teleportation points.
Implementation Details: Check if the player has a teleport ability or item. When triggered, move the player’s position to a specified location (cursor, marker, or predefined teleport spot). Commonly balanced by cooldowns, resource costs, or line of sight. Be mindful of collision checks and not placing the player inside walls.

Name: Dash (Grounded)
Description: A rapid burst of movement on the ground, typically covering a short distance quickly or letting the player reposition. Often on a cooldown or limited usage.
Implementation Details: Unlike an air dash, this happens when the player is on the floor. Apply a higher-than-normal horizontal velocity for a short duration, then revert to normal. Commonly includes a visual effect and possible invincibility frames.

Name: Phase Shift
Description: Entering a different state or dimension where the character can pass through certain objects or is immune to certain hazards. Movement may or may not be affected differently.
Implementation Details: Trigger a phase mode that flags the player as intangible to specific collision layers or hazards. Keep track of a timer or resource draining while in phase shift. Revert to normal after the timer ends or resource depletes.

Name: Swinging (With ropes or vines)
Description: Attaching to a pivot point (rope, vine, chain) and moving in an arc under gravity to gain momentum. Letting go at the right time can launch the player.
Implementation Details: Detect when the player grabs onto a rope or vine (overlap or collision). While attached, disable normal movement, apply a pivot-based physics system or a pseudo-swing using trigonometry. Releasing the input detaches the player, preserving momentum.

Name: Gliding / Paragliding
Description: Slowing the character’s descent, allowing controlled movement in the air for an extended duration. Often triggered after a jump or fall by holding a dedicated glide button.
Implementation Details: If the player is in mid-air and toggles the glide input, reduce the effect of gravity or clamp downward velocity. The player can move horizontally more freely, but usually at a limited rate. End gliding if the player lands or releases the input.

Name: Hover / Float
Description: Maintaining a certain height or hovering in the air for a short time. Slows horizontal falling or keeps the character at a near-constant vertical position.
Implementation Details: When hovering is activated, reduce or zero out gravity while the key is held, or for a set duration. Often used for precise positioning in the air or crossing short gaps. Can be limited by a meter or cooldown.

Name: Flying (Full Aerial Control)
Description: Gives complete freedom of movement in the air, often limited by a resource or a special power-up. Can move in any direction without falling.
Implementation Details: Disable or reduce gravity entirely and allow the player to move in all directions. Speed may be capped, and a stamina meter might drain while flying. Restored upon landing or waiting.

Name: Aerial Surfing / Hoverboard
Description: Standing on a device that maintains forward momentum in the air, allowing unique aerial maneuvers. The board may have limited turning and relies on momentum.
Implementation Details: When the player is on the hoverboard, override normal jump or flight physics. Implement a forward velocity, some lift to counter gravity, and limited directional control. Possibly add friction or inertia to simulate a board feel.

Name: Swimming
Description: Movement in water is generally slower and more buoyant than on land. The player can move in all directions, but with reduced speed and inertia.
Implementation Details: Detect if the player is in water. Reduce gravity or apply upward buoyancy. Allow for multi-directional movement but typically slower than land movement. Possibly track oxygen/breath if the head is submerged.

Name: Diving/Submerging
Description: Going beneath the water’s surface, typically toggling a breath meter or oxygen limit. Movement becomes fully aquatic, with added pressure or slower movement.
Implementation Details: Track whether the player is above or below the water line. When diving, switch to swimming mechanics entirely. Decrease oxygen over time, and if oxygen hits zero, trigger damage or drowning.

Name: Surfacing
Description: Returning to the water’s surface from below to restore air/breath or exit the aquatic environment. Often involves a transition back to normal movement.
Implementation Details: When the player’s head intersects the water’s surface from below, reset oxygen and switch to normal gravity. Possibly trigger a ‘breach’ animation. Careful collision checks ensure smooth transition.

Name: Underwater Boost
Description: Using special propulsion while submerged (jets, flippers, or submersible vehicles) for rapid underwater movement, bypassing the slower default swim speed.
Implementation Details: If the player has a power-up or is in a submersible vehicle, significantly increase horizontal and vertical speed underwater. Possibly add a fuel or energy gauge that depletes on boost usage.

Name: Mount/Vehicles
Description: Riding animals or operating vehicles for faster or specialized movement. Can offer protection, different physics, or unique combat abilities.
Implementation Details: When mounting, replace or override the player’s normal movement with mount/vehicle physics. The mount may have its own speed, health, or controls (e.g., accelerating, steering). Dismounting restores the player’s standard state. Possibly track a separate hitbox or collision for the mount.

Name: Zip-to-Target (Homing Lunge)
Description: A rapid approach or leap toward a targeted enemy or point, typically with a lock-on mechanic. Often used for quickly closing distance or chaining attacks.
Implementation Details: Upon input, find the nearest enemy or a locked-on target. Temporarily override player movement with a direct, fast approach to that position. May include auto-tracking so you land precisely on the target. Could have a cooldown or resource cost.

Name: Hiding / Sneaking
Description: Slow and quiet movement aimed at avoiding detection by enemies or security systems. Often combined with crouching or environmental cover.
Implementation Details: When sneaking, reduce movement speed, footstep sounds, and visibility. Could be triggered by a dedicated key or automatically when in shadows. Some games use a detection meter that fills more slowly if you’re sneaking.

Name: Light/Basic Attacks
Description: Quick strikes with minimal damage but faster recovery. Often used to initiate combos or safely poke at enemies.
Implementation Details: When the player presses the attack button, play a short animation and check collision or overlap with enemies. Apply small damage. Quick cooldown or short wind-up allows repeated use.

Name: Heavy/Charged Attacks
Description: Slower but more powerful strikes, often involving a wind-up or charge period. Deals higher damage or can break enemy guards.
Implementation Details: On holding the attack button, begin charging. Increase damage up to a cap. On release, perform the strike with a big damage value or special effect. Vulnerable to interruption during the wind-up.

Name: Combo Chains
Description: A sequence of attacks performed in rapid succession, each possibly dealing incremental damage or culminating in a finisher. Timing input windows are important.
Implementation Details: Track the current combo step and a short time window to accept the next input. If pressed within the window, progress to the next step. Each step has a unique animation and damage profile. If time runs out, reset the combo.

Name: Ranged Shots
Description: Firing projectiles or using hitscan weapons (bullets, arrows, etc.) to attack from a distance. Damage and accuracy can vary based on weapon type.
Implementation Details: On ranged input, create a projectile sprite or raycast from the player’s position in the aimed direction. Check for collisions or hits along the trajectory. Different weapons may have different speeds, arcs, or spread.

Name: Magic Spells
Description: Elemental or arcane attacks that often consume mana or have cooldowns. Can produce various effects like fireballs, lightning bolts, healing, etc.
Implementation Details: Track a mana or spell resource. On spell input, check if sufficient mana is available. Spawn a spell projectile or effect. Subtract mana and set a cooldown if necessary. Different spells might have unique visuals and damage types.

Name: AoE Blasts
Description: Area-of-effect explosions or shockwaves that damage multiple targets in a radius. Often used for crowd control or clearing groups of enemies.
Implementation Details: When triggered, instantiate an AoE effect at the target location. Check all enemies within the defined radius; apply damage or knockback. Could require a resource cost or have a long cooldown.

Name: Summoning
Description: Calling forth allies or creatures to fight alongside the player. Summons can have their own AI, health, and damage output.
Implementation Details: On summon input, check resources (mana, special item). Instantiate an allied entity and set its behaviors (follow player or attack enemies). Summons may persist until defeated or a time limit ends.

Name: Weapon Modes/Alternate Fire
Description: Switching a weapon between different firing types (single-shot, burst, spread, charged beam, etc.). Each mode may have unique ammo consumption or effects.
Implementation Details: On mode switch input, cycle the weapon’s firing pattern. The firing code checks the current mode to determine projectile type, rate of fire, or damage. Each mode might have its own sound/animation.

Name: Grab & Throw
Description: Grappling an opponent or object, then tossing it away. Can be used for crowd control, puzzle-solving, or environmental kills.
Implementation Details: When in range, initiate a grab state if the opponent/object is grabbable. While grabbed, the target is attached to the player’s position. On throw input, apply a force to the target and release it, dealing damage if it hits a wall or another enemy.

Name: Takedowns/Stealth Kills
Description: One-hit eliminations performed from stealth or behind. Often silent, preventing alerting nearby enemies.
Implementation Details: Check if the player is behind an enemy or undetected. When triggered, play a special animation and instantly reduce the enemy’s health to zero or a critical state. Could trigger alarms if witnessed by other guards.

Name: Critical/Weak Point Attacks
Description: Hitting a vulnerable spot on an enemy to deal extra damage. This can be a timed mechanic or an aim-based system (e.g., headshots).
Implementation Details: Mark certain enemy areas as weak points (e.g., head collider). On hit detection, if the attack lands on that collider, multiply damage by a factor. Some enemies might have different weak points or states.

Name: Finishing Moves
Description: A special high-damage or instant-kill attack triggered under specific conditions (low enemy health, stun state, etc.). Often cinematic or accompanied by a flourish.
Implementation Details: When an enemy’s health falls below a threshold or they enter a staggered state, the player can perform a finisher. Briefly lock both the player and enemy in an animation, then deal massive damage or an instant kill.

Name: Splash/Spread Attacks
Description: Strikes or shots that affect multiple targets in a cone or line, spreading out from the source. Often used for crowd control or multi-hits.
Implementation Details: On attack trigger, define an arc or cone in front of the player. Any enemy within that cone receives damage. For projectiles, spawn multiple projectiles at slightly different angles. Great for shotguns or wide-swing weapons.

Name: Headshots/Precision Hits
Description: Aiming at an enemy’s head or vital spot for extra damage. Typically used in shooters or ranged combat systems.
Implementation Details: Give enemies a smaller head collider or define a bounding box for the head region. If a projectile or raycast hits that region, apply a damage multiplier. Often pairs with a crosshair or reticle for aiming feedback.

Name: Elemental Weapons
Description: Infusing attacks with elemental properties like fire, ice, poison, or lightning. Can add status effects or special damage types.
Implementation Details: If the player’s weapon is imbued with an element, apply additional effects on hit (burning, freezing, etc.). Track duration of status or apply immediate bonus damage. Each element might have different effects and visuals.

Name: Weapon Overheat/System Strain
Description: High-intensity usage causes the weapon or system to overheat or strain, temporarily locking it or reducing efficiency until it cools down.
Implementation Details: Track a heat or strain meter that increases with each attack or shot. If it reaches the limit, the weapon is disabled for a cooldown period. Gradually decrease the meter over time when not firing.

Name: Chain Lightning / Ricochet
Description: Projectiles or spells that bounce from one target to another, striking multiple enemies in quick succession.
Implementation Details: Upon hitting an enemy, locate the next closest enemy within a certain range. Spawn a new projectile or automatically arc to that target. Continue until a max chain count or no more targets are in range.

Name: Projectile Reflection
Description: Reflecting or parrying enemy shots back at them with precise timing or a shield/weapon ability. The projectile changes direction and can harm its original owner.
Implementation Details: On a well-timed block or parry, invert the projectile’s velocity or redirect it toward the shooter. Possibly enhance damage or ensure it hits the original enemy. Requires collision or overlap checks to detect the moment of reflection.

Name: Leech/Lifesteal Attacks
Description: Attacks that restore a portion of the damage dealt as health to the attacker. Often limited to specific weapons, spells, or conditions.
Implementation Details: If a weapon or spell has a lifesteal property, a fraction of the damage inflicted on enemies is added back to the player's health. Keep track of the player’s max health to avoid overhealing. Possibly have diminishing returns.

Name: Parrying
Description: A perfectly timed block or deflection that stuns or staggers the attacker, creating an opening for a counter.
Implementation Details: Requires precise timing when the enemy's attack is about to land. If the player activates parry within the right window, the enemy is staggered. In some systems, the player takes no damage on a successful parry. Parrying might consume stamina or have a cooldown.

Name: Guard Breaks
Description: A strong move specifically designed to break through an opponent’s block, leaving them briefly vulnerable.
Implementation Details: When a player is in a block state, certain heavy or charged attacks can force a guard break if they connect. This may instantly drain a ‘guard meter’ or cause a stun, making the defender unable to block for a moment.

Name: Defensive Stance/Mode
Description: A stance or mode that boosts defense or reduces damage taken. The player moves slower or deals less damage in return.
Implementation Details: Activating a defensive stance can alter movement speed, damage output, and damage intake. Often toggled on/off or maintained as long as a button is held, draining stamina or resource over time.

Name: Magical Barriers
Description: Temporary protective fields that absorb incoming hits or provide immunity to certain effects. Often visualized as a glowing shield around the character.
Implementation Details: Upon activation, create a barrier with a health value or duration. The barrier might negate all damage until it is depleted or expires. Could be single-element (e.g., fire shield) or universal. Might cost mana or have a cooldown.

Name: Armor Systems
Description: Passive damage reduction or extra health provided by equipped gear. Armor can degrade over time or be bypassed by specific attacks.
Implementation Details: Assign an armor value that reduces incoming damage by a percentage or fixed amount. If the game includes degradation, reduce armor durability each time the player is hit. Armor breaks when durability reaches zero.

Name: Elemental Resistances
Description: Reduced damage from certain elemental or magical attacks, often tied to equipment or character traits (e.g., fire resistance).
Implementation Details: Track resistance values for each element (e.g., fire, ice, lightning). When an attack with that element hits the player, multiply the damage by (1 - resistance). Resistances can be gained from gear or buffs and can stack with other defensive mechanics.

Name: Regenerative Shields
Description: A shield layer that regenerates over time if the player avoids taking damage for a set period. Common in modern shooters or sci-fi settings.
Implementation Details: Give the player a shield value and a timer that resets each time they take damage. If the timer finishes, replenish the shield at a certain rate until it’s full or the player is hit again.

Name: Cover Mechanics
Description: Using the environment (walls, crates, etc.) to block line of sight or incoming fire. Typically seen in shooter games, allowing players to pop in/out of cover for attacks.
Implementation Details: Identify cover objects in the level. When the player is near a cover object and presses the cover button, they snap to a position behind it. While in cover, reduce or negate damage from certain angles. The player can peek out or fire from cover.

Name: Healing/Support Skills
Description: Abilities or spells that restore health or provide buffs. Can be self-targeted or applied to allies in co-op or team-based games.
Implementation Details: When the skill is used, the player or target gains health over time or instantly. Some skills have an area of effect to heal multiple allies. Usually consumes mana, items, or has cooldowns.

Name: Dodge Roll/Evade Step
Description: A quick movement to avoid attacks, typically granting brief invincibility frames (i-frames). Often used in action or RPG combat.
Implementation Details: On dodge input, the character swiftly moves or rolls in the chosen direction. During a short time window, the character can't be damaged. Then normal movement resumes. Often has a cooldown or stamina cost.

Name: Sidestep/Strafe
Description: Rapid horizontal movement to avoid linear attacks or reposition, commonly seen in 3D action or shooter games.
Implementation Details: When a sidestep input is pressed, push the character quickly sideways without changing facing direction. In top-down or 3D, maintain aim while moving laterally. Usually short distance, with a brief speed boost.

Name: Teleport Dodge
Description: Instantly blink a short distance to evade attacks. Similar to a dodge roll but without traversing the space in-between.
Implementation Details: On dodge input, if the teleport ability is available, move the player to a new position (e.g., a few tiles or units away) instantly. Often includes i-frames during or right after the teleport.

Name: Jump/Dash Cancel
Description: Canceling an ongoing attack or action by quickly jumping or dashing, allowing advanced mobility and combo extensions.
Implementation Details: If the game allows it, at certain frames of an attack, the player can input jump or dash to interrupt the animation. This can lead to more fluid combos or quick escapes. Usually restricted to certain moves or states.

Name: Slide/Slip
Description: A low-profile movement, often from running or dashing, letting the player move under attacks or obstacles. Can also help reposition quickly.
Implementation Details: While running, the player presses a button to initiate a slide. The character’s hitbox is lowered, evading high attacks. After a short distance or time, the slide ends. Often has limited turning and momentum-based stopping.

Name: Aerial Evade/Double Jump
Description: An additional mid-air jump or quick maneuver to avoid aerial threats. Different from multi-jump used for platforming; it’s more defensive in nature.
Implementation Details: If the player is airborne and an evade input is pressed, allow one quick direction change or jump. This might consume a resource or only be available once per air time. Grants i-frames or a burst of movement.

Name: Phase/Intangible Shift
Description: Temporarily becoming intangible or ghost-like, letting the character pass through enemies or evade attacks entirely.
Implementation Details: When activated, disable collisions with certain layers or set the player’s hitbox to ignore damage. This mode typically lasts a short time and might consume a unique resource. Reverts automatically or upon a second input.

Name: Manual Aim
Description: Full control of aiming, often with a crosshair or reticle. Accuracy depends on player skill and crosshair control.
Implementation Details: In 2D or 3D, read mouse/joystick input and rotate a reticle or camera accordingly. Projectiles or raycasts are fired in the direction of the reticle. No auto-correction or snapping is applied.

Name: Soft Lock-On
Description: The reticle or aim loosely snaps to nearby enemies, but the player can still fine-tune aim. Common in console shooters to assist with gamepad controls.
Implementation Details: When the player aims near an enemy, shift the reticle slightly towards that enemy. Maintain a small radius or angle threshold for the snap. If the player aims away, the lock is lost.

Name: Hard Lock-On
Description: The camera and attacks remain focused on a selected target, typical in action RPGs or hack-and-slash games. Player movement orbits the locked target.
Implementation Details: On lock-on input, pick the nearest enemy. The camera or targeting system automatically tracks that enemy. Movement inputs may pivot around them. Attacks or spells automatically aim at the locked target until lock is released.

Name: Aim Assist
Description: A mild correction for the player’s aim, often found in console shooters. Slows reticle movement near targets or slightly magnetizes bullets to the enemy.
Implementation Details: While the crosshair is near an enemy, reduce the aiming sensitivity or apply a small auto-correction. Bullets or rays might have a small cone that nudges towards nearby targets, making it easier to hit. It's subtler than a soft lock.

Name: AoE Targeting Circle
Description: Marking an area on the ground or in space where a spell or explosive will land. Often used for bombs, artillery, or large spells.
Implementation Details: When selecting an AoE skill, show a circle or indicator at the target position (using mouse position or lock-on). On confirmation, deal damage to all units within the radius. The circle might be dynamic, letting the player adjust it before committing.

Name: Projectile Leading
Description: Aiming assistance that accounts for target movement by indicating where to shoot so a projectile can intercept the target. Common in vehicle or sci-fi shooters.
Implementation Details: Calculate an intercept point based on the target’s velocity and the projectile’s speed. Display a lead reticle so the player knows where to fire. Update dynamically if the target changes direction or speed.

Name: Multi-Target Lock
Description: Locking onto multiple enemies at once to fire homing missiles or chain attacks. Often used in flying shooters or advanced targeting systems.
Implementation Details: When holding the lock-on button, cycle through nearby enemies in the reticle. Each locked target gets a marker. On release, launch projectiles that home in on each locked target. Limit the number of locks possible.

Name: Poison/Bleed
Description: Applies a status effect that continuously drains health over time. Bleed is often associated with physical wounds, while poison might be a toxin effect.
Implementation Details: When inflicted, apply a debuff that periodically reduces the target’s health for a set duration or until cured. You can track it with a timer or a stack system (multiple applications for higher damage). Typically, poison/bleed won't outright kill a target past 1 HP in some games, but this can vary by design.

Name: Burn/Fire Damage
Description: Targets are ignited, taking continuous damage or igniting flammable surfaces around them. May also cause panic or reduce accuracy in some games.
Implementation Details: Similar to poison, but with a fire theme—often deals faster or burst ticks of damage. Can spread to the environment if flammable surfaces or chain reactions are possible. Might destroy certain obstacles or cause additional effects (e.g., lighting up dark areas).

Name: Stun/Daze
Description: Renders an enemy unable to act or significantly slows their reactions, making them vulnerable to attacks. Often represented by a star-ringing or swirling effect.
Implementation Details: When stunned, an enemy cannot move, attack, or defend for a duration. Track a stun timer and ignore AI inputs. Some games allow reduced control (e.g., slow movement) rather than total immobilization.

Name: Freeze/Slow
Description: Significantly reduces an enemy’s movement speed or locks them completely in place if fully frozen. Some games allow shattering a frozen foe with a heavy hit.
Implementation Details: When an enemy is frozen or slowed, modify their velocity or AI movement speeds. Fully frozen targets may lose all actions. Could use a separate thaw timer or break free mechanic. Partial slow can reduce attack speed and movement.

Name: Mind Control/Charm
Description: Temporarily turns enemies into allies, causing them to fight for or protect the player. Duration or success chance may vary.
Implementation Details: When charmed, switch the enemy’s allegiance to the player’s side. Change their AI behavior to attack their former allies. After the effect ends, revert them to hostile. Watch for balancing issues if large groups are charmed.

Name: Defense/Offense Debuffs
Description: Lowering enemy stats (like armor or attack power), making them weaker or more vulnerable to incoming damage.
Implementation Details: When applied, reduce specific enemy attributes (e.g., -20% defense). Track a duration. Once expired, restore original values. Multiple debuffs can stack, but be mindful of stacking rules to avoid excessive layering.

Name: Buffs
Description: Increasing a character’s attributes or granting special effects (e.g., increased speed, damage, or defense).
Implementation Details: Similar to debuffs, but beneficial for the player or allies. Apply the effect for a duration (e.g., +20% attack). Remove or fade the effect after the timer. Effects can stack if the design allows it.

Name: Stamina/Endurance
Description: A resource that depletes with actions like attacking, dodging, or sprinting, and recovers over time or when resting. Prevents spamming powerful moves.
Implementation Details: Whenever the player performs a stamina-costing action, subtract from their stamina pool. If it’s too low, actions are blocked or less effective. Stamina recharges gradually. Speed of recovery can be modified by rest or items.

Name: Mana/Energy
Description: A resource consumed by spells or special moves. Functions similarly to stamina but typically tied to magical or ranged abilities.
Implementation Details: Track a mana/energy pool. Each spell or skill has a set cost. If not enough mana is available, the skill can’t be cast. Often recovers slowly or via items. Some games allow partial casts or color-coded resources for different magic types.

Name: Ammo & Reloading
Description: Limited ammunition for ranged weapons, requiring reloading or resource management. Reloading can be manual or automatic when empty.
Implementation Details: Each weapon tracks its current ammo in the magazine and total reserve ammo. Firing reduces the magazine ammo. If it hits zero, trigger a reload animation or action. Reloading refills from reserves if available.

Name: Cooldown Timers
Description: Prevents spammable skills by requiring a waiting period after each use. Common for abilities, spells, or items.
Implementation Details: Each skill has a cooldown value. When used, set the skill’s cooldown timer. The skill can’t be used again until it has fully recharged. Often represented by a cooldown bar or icon overlay.

Name: Overheat Gauges
Description: A bar that fills with continuous use of a weapon or ability. Once maxed, it triggers a forced cooldown or reduced performance.
Implementation Details: Similar to the concept of a heat meter. Each shot or action increases heat. If the gauge reaches max, the system locks up or performance drops until it cools down. Cooling may be passive over time or manual (e.g., venting).

Name: Environmental Hazards
Description: Using parts of the environment like lava, spikes, or explosive objects to damage or hinder enemies. Often can harm the player too if misused.
Implementation Details: Place hazard objects or zones in the level. If an entity overlaps or triggers them, apply damage or a harmful effect. Could be a static hazard (lava pit) or dynamic (falling rocks). Some hazards might be triggered by the player.

Name: Destructible Cover
Description: Walls, crates, or barriers that can be destroyed to expose or flank enemies. Adds a dynamic element to level design.
Implementation Details: Assign health to cover objects. When the object’s health is reduced to zero, spawn debris and remove the cover collision or sprite. Possibly trigger chain reactions if it’s explosive or structural (collapsing entire areas).

Name: Cliff/Edge Tactics
Description: Knocking enemies off a ledge or into a pit for an instant or high-damage defeat. Encourages positioning strategies.
Implementation Details: If an enemy is near a ledge and takes a strong knockback, they can fall off. This may kill them outright or deal massive fall damage. Some enemies or bosses might be immune or can fly back.

Name: Traps & Mines
Description: Placable or pre-set traps that detonate or activate when enemies step on them or come within range.
Implementation Details: When a trap is placed, it becomes armed after a short delay. Any enemy (or player, if friendly fire is a thing) stepping on it triggers an explosion or effect. The trap is consumed or destroyed after activation.

Name: Use of Terrain
Description: Taking advantage of high ground, choke points, or environmental features for strategic benefit (e.g., vantage points or funneling enemies).
Implementation Details: Design levels with varied elevation and cover. For example, shooting from high ground might increase range or accuracy. Choke points limit enemy approach. The game code can apply buffs or allow special vantage-based attacks when on elevated terrain.

Name: Pick Up/Collect
Description: Acquiring items, power-ups, or resources in the game world to store in inventory or use immediately.
Implementation Details: When the player overlaps with an item collider, trigger a pickup event. The item is removed from the world, and the player’s inventory or stats are updated. May play a sound or animation. Some items might be automatically collected or require a button press.

Name: Drop/Place
Description: Removing an item from your inventory or placing it into the game world for later use or strategic positioning.
Implementation Details: If an item is in the player’s possession, allow a drop action. Instantiate the item in the world at the player’s location. For placeable objects (like traps or bombs), position them with an offset or alignment logic. May require confirmation or specific surfaces.

Name: Push/Pull
Description: Moving objects or enemies around in the environment, often for puzzle-solving or creating strategic advantages (e.g., pushing a block onto a switch).
Implementation Details: Allow the player to press against movable objects or use a special action to grip them. Adjust the object’s velocity or position based on player input. For pulling enemies, you might have a grapple that drags them towards the player.

Name: Throw/Lob
Description: Propelling an object (or weapon) in an arc or straight line. Can be used to hit distant targets, place items at a distance, or cause damage on impact.
Implementation Details: When throwing, apply an initial velocity to the object, often with an arc if it’s a lobbed throw. If it hits an enemy, deal damage or trigger an effect. Some items break on impact; others might bounce or remain in the environment.

Name: Rotate/Turn
Description: Adjusting an object’s orientation in the game world for puzzle alignment (e.g., turning a statue to face a certain direction).
Implementation Details: When interacting with a rotatable object, allow the player to change its angle or orientation. This might open doors, align mirrors for light puzzles, or connect pathways. In a grid-based system, each press rotates 90 degrees; in free rotation, read input to turn continuously.

Name: Combine/Craft
Description: Merging multiple items to create a new one (e.g., combining herbs, parts for a weapon upgrade, etc.). Often done in an inventory or crafting menu.
Implementation Details: Check if the player has the required components. On confirm, remove them from inventory and add the crafted item. Some systems allow recipes or experimentation for unknown combinations.

Name: Break/Smash
Description: Destroying objects like crates, jars, or other breakables to obtain hidden items or clear pathways. Common in many action/adventure games.
Implementation Details: When the player attacks or interacts with a breakable object, it shatters if enough damage is dealt, spawning item drops or leaving behind debris. May also block access to certain areas until smashed.

Name: Inspect/Examine
Description: Looking closely at an object, reading lore text, or revealing details that might be used for puzzle solutions or story progression.
Implementation Details: When the player interacts with an examinable object, display a UI panel or message about it. Possibly highlight interactive areas or clues. Some items might require rotating the camera around them for hidden details.

Name: Lockpicking/Unlocking
Description: Using a skill or tool to bypass locked doors or chests. Often involves a mini-game or chance-based system. Alternatively, a key item instantly unlocks.
Implementation Details: When encountering a locked object, check if the player has the required key or initiates a lockpick mini-game. Success opens the lock; failure can break lockpicks or trigger alarms. Some locks require a certain skill level or puzzle solution.

Name: Repair
Description: Fixing damaged gear, machinery, or structures. Restores functionality or durability. May require specific tools or resources.
Implementation Details: When repair is initiated, check if the player has the required materials or skill level. If yes, fix or restore durability to the object. Could involve a short repair animation or progress bar. In some games, partial repairs are possible.

Name: Upgrade/Enhance
Description: Improving an item’s stats or adding special properties (e.g., forging a sword to increase damage, adding elemental effects, or customizing parts).
